Thinking about design here - in terms of prefix definitions, would the cnd file take precedence, in case there's an overlap of prefixes with different definitions (ie, ones from the existing model in the system vs ones in the file)?  Seems like what's
the system should take precedence over the file.  Really, just thinking about how to do this in a clear way so users aren't then confused in a different way.

, yes, I think the CND file would take precedence.  Though given the issues that have surfaced in the 4.7.0/4.7.2 upgrades, I think that defining custom namespaces in the CND file might not be a good idea.  If users can post RDF with their own namespaces, then they would not need to update the CND file in order to have control over their namespaces.

I created an object in 4.7-maintenance using Turtle with namespaces defined, and saw the old behavior as expected (ns001 etc. namespaces were used instead).

over to my branch, rebuilt, and did an update to the object I created, using my namespace definitions from before, without problems (the ns001 prefixes were still used in the output, my update was applied).  I then made further updates with new namespaces and their prefixes were used as expected.

In Fedora 4.5.0 and before, when a new namespace was observed in RDF with namespace prefixes (e.g., turtle), the user-supplied namespace prefix was registered and used in subsequent uses of that namespace.  If the user did not supply a prefix, or was using an RDF serialization without prefixes (e.g., ntriples), then Fedora generated a prefix like ns001.
Since Fedora 4.5.1, Fedora ignores any user-supplied prefix and always generates a prefix like ns001.

comments.body:
Potential source of this change:
https://jira.duraspace.org/browse/FCREPO-1312

  • https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/commit/523953db47ff09c0311de1dd51e98ae384cc0836#diff-7aee50d5030524028026aa94cd75f350L554
  • https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/commit/523953db47ff09c0311de1dd51e98ae384cc0836#diff-f5973302ab00a1fb20d9fe8cace27e3bR59

Those changes to RdfAdder and FedoraResourceImpl are part of the problem — and the other part is removing the call to model.getNsPrefixMap().  It looks easy to get the prefix mapping from the input model and pass it into RdfAdder (which is currently get namespaces from the JCR session and not looking for any input namespaces).

Thinking about design here - in terms of prefix definitions, would the cnd file take precedence, in case there's an overlap of prefixes with different definitions (ie, ones from the existing model in the system vs ones in the file)?  Seems like what's in the system should take precedence over the file.  Really, just thinking about how to do this in a clear way so users aren't then confused in a different way.

Bethany Seeger, yes, I think the CND file would take precedence.  Though given the issues that have surfaced in the 4.7.0/4.7.2 upgrades, I think that defining custom namespaces in the CND file might not be a good idea.  If users can post RDF with their own namespaces, then they would not need to update the CND file in order to have control over their namespaces.

https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1195

This PR works fine for me with parallelism turned off, but fails on Travis with parallelism on.  See https://jira.duraspace.org/browse/FCREPO-2466

Yes, I've rebased https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1195 and it passes with parallel builds enabled now that the underlying parallelism issue has been resolved.
Thanks, Esmé Cowles, looks good... pending response to one minor comment.

I created an object in 4.7-maintenance using Turtle with namespaces defined, and saw the old behavior as expected (ns001 etc. namespaces were used instead).

I then cherry-picked https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/commit/81be86f4809be5620a0f74a5c5c6de6819169fea over to my branch, rebuilt, and did an update to the object I created, using my namespace definitions from before, without problems (the ns001 prefixes were still used in the output, my update was applied).  I then made further updates with new namespaces and their prefixes were used as expected.
